say: Pulse anatomy. The lifecycle of one request, from bytes on disk, to the JSON envelope.
Every cohort is one self-describing file. It opens with a nine-byte header: eight magic bytes, then a format version.
Next comes the schema block. It names every field with its type, whether it can be null, its byte offset and its bit position.
Dictionaries for categorical and set fields sit inline, so every stored code can be read back as its label.
Then come the records, each one exactly the same width. So Pulse counts records with simple arithmetic: payload length, divided by stride.
A request is admitted gate by gate. The feature-profile check and item fan-out need nothing but the request itself.
Opening the cohort reads only the header and the schema. With the schema in hand, smart defaults infer the grouper type the request left out.
Field references, weights and resource limits are all checked against the schema alone. Watch the counter: not one record has been read.
Now a second request asks for more memory than this instance allows. The limits preflight refuses it, with zero records decoded.
This cohort turns out to be a shard archive: four pulse shards, under one canonical schema. Now the engine chooses how to run.
Every operator in this request can merge its state, so the work fans out, with one worker per shard.
Inside each worker, records stream through the loop one at a time. The decoder reads only the three columns the request actually names.
A range filter drops anyone outside eighteen to sixty-five, and counts what passed, and what didn't. Those counts become components of the response.
A formula attribute adds income in thousands. The category grouper routes each record by region, and the average aggregator updates its running state.
The streaming arm keeps no rows at all, just state: four buckets, each holding a count and a mean.
Each shard runs that same loop over its own records, with fresh operator state.
The workers finish whenever they finish. Here, shard three is first, then one, four, and two.
But partials always merge in shard order, never finish order, so the result matches a serial run exactly.
In a crosstab, each record lands in the cell where its row key and its column key meet.
Record two has a region, but no plan, so it never reaches a cell. Yet the East margin, and the grand total, still count it.
Margins are recomputed from raw rows. Auxiliary margins admit only the records that reached a cell.
Now the response assembles: result rows first, then components, which count exactly what each figure stands on.
Tests report a raw p-value. The multiplicity fold adds an adjusted p-value beside it and never overwrites the original.
An overlay attaches as a read-only sibling, keyed to the rows it describes. The data itself is untouched.
Return shaping removes whatever the caller excluded. An excluded part is absent from the output, not null.
Finally, the envelope wraps it all: format version one point one, the data, and errors and warnings that are always lists.
That is the life of a Pulse request. Open, admit, check, choose an arm, loop, merge, fold, shape, and wrap.
